Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson is doubling down on buying the selloff after the S&P 500 broke below his 7,100 downside target. In Monday's note, his team called it "the fat pitch we have patiently been waiting for, and we're not going to miss it," adding that "markets bottom on bad news and deleveraging. We have had a lot of both" (via Bloomberg).

How we got here:

▪️ In late September, he warned of a drop to as low as 7,100 before the bull market resumed.
▪️ In early November, he said the correction was in its final innings, with a 7,100 to 7,300 range. On November 16, he raised his 12-month target to 8,700.
▪️ On Friday, the S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39, 2.7% below the bottom of that range and 11.6% below the October 6 record. That capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest since February 2020.

Why he's pressing the call rather than backing off:

▪️ He calls the break below his range an overshoot of fair value, driven by forced deleveraging. His team is more bullish tactically than at any time since early April.
▪️ Sentiment: his sentiment indicator hit −1.6 and the VIX hit 36, both matching December 2018, and hedge fund positioning is similarly washed out.
▪️ Valuation: the S&P 500's forward P/E has dropped from nearly 23 in late October to 16.5, below its 17.4 long-run average. The Nasdaq 100 is under 17, below its pandemic low.
▪️ Earnings: by his math, stocks are pricing in about a 6% drop in 2027 earnings. He forecasts 14% growth, and consensus is 17%.
▪️ He likes hyperscalers, industrials, quality cyclicals with improving estimates, and companies benefiting from AI adoption.
▪️ The main risk is still a hawkish Fed. But he thinks market pricing is "far too hawkish" and expects a calmer message in December than some fear.

The history backs him, with a catch. Since 1990, the VIX has had 17 episodes where it first closed at 35 or higher (Friday's close was 35.89):

▪️ The S&P 500 was higher 12 months later in 14 of the 17, with a median gain of 21.6%. That compares with 11.9% for any 12-month stretch since 1990.
▪️ December 2018, the episode he compares this one to, was followed by a 37.1% gain.
▪️ But the first spike often wasn't the low. In 8 of the 17, the S&P 500 fell more than 5% further within three months, including another 34.9% in 2008 and 24.9% in 2020.
▪️ The three losing years were 2001 and 2008, both earnings recessions, and 2022, a Fed hiking cycle.

History would indicate his call should hold unless earnings roll over or the Fed gets much more aggressive. The market is already pricing in an earnings drop he doesn't expect, so the bigger swing factor is the Fed, the one risk he concedes. 

Morgan Stanley chief economist Seth Carpenter acknowledged in his Sunday Start note (via ZeroHedge) that clients pushed back hard on the bank's "Embracing Risk" outlook, and that even if the bank is right, the path through 2027 "will not be smooth or linear."
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson (Strategy Data Pack, Friday) says the S&P 500 “catching down” to weaker breadth “is likely the final stage of this correction," after he rightly called a continuation of the pullback in semi's in the event of a big Democratic victory.

But he isn’t calling the bottom yet: “We are getting close, but would like to see… further confirmation from our sentiment indicator.” His year-end target stays 8,000.

Here's what’s happened to the three “clearing events” he laid out last weekend:

▪️ Midterms: Democrats took both chambers, with at least 54 Senate seats. Wilson had said a 52-48 Senate was priced in but 55-45 wasn’t, and that a bigger margin could fuel pushback on data centers, so he nailed that.
▪️ AI and semis: Thursday was the S&P’s worst day since April 2025 (−4.4%) and the Nasdaq-100’s worst since March 2020 (−6.4%). The SOX fell about 12% on weak chip guidance and fears of data-center rules after the election. That left it down about 19% from October 26, when Wilson called for another 10% to 15% drop into mid-November, another hit.
▪️ Liquidity, the one he ranks most important, hasn’t cleared. He says Fed Chair Warsh acknowledged financial conditions are doing some of the Fed’s tightening but wouldn’t call them “tight,” so the bar for a dovish pivot “remains high.” Then Friday’s payrolls (+165,000 vs. ~65,000 expected) pushed December hike odds to about 78%.

The math from Friday’s close of 7,376.86 (−5.7% from the record, −2.7% on the week):
▪️ 7,100 to 7,200 is another 2.4% to 3.8% down.
▪️ 8,000 is +8.4% from here. His 12-month base case is 8,300 (+12.5%), with a 5,900 bear case and 9,400 bull case.

On the catch-down, as he also indicated was likely, the average stock is holding up better than the index:
▪️ Thursday, the equal-weight S&P fell 2.9% vs. 4.4% for the cap-weighted index.
▪️ In October, equal-weight beat cap-weight by 5.9 points, the second-widest monthly gap since 2003.
▪️ Wilson notes median Russell 3000 earnings growth is running 14%, the strongest in four years.

His sentiment indicator was at −0.75 as of Thursday. That compares with roughly −1.45 at the Iran-war low earlier this year and about −2.1 on Liberation Day.

Composite 54.6 (October 55.9)
Manufacturing 54.5 (est 54.6; October 54.9)
Services 54.7 (est 55.8; October 56.1)

Growth cooled to the slowest since July but stayed solid, with S&P calling it “sustained strong economic growth.”

Activity and demand:
▪️ Composite at a four-month low; manufacturing PMI at a three-month low, still improving for a 16th straight month; services at a four-month low.
▪️ New orders grew at the weakest pace since July, “led by a marked slowing of new business inflows into the service sector” on uncertainty, high prices and higher interest rates.
▪️ Exports fell for the first time in four months.

Capacity:
▪️ Backlogs rose again in both manufacturing and services on “constrained operating capacity.”
▪️ Hiring was “the joint-third largest seen for over four years,” with factory job creation “the second-strongest since July 2021.”
▪️ Supplier delivery times lengthened the most since August 2022, tied to “global trade disruptions,” especially for metals and electronics.

Prices:
▪️ Selling price inflation cooled after October’s rise, the largest since August 2022, with “manufacturing selling prices rising especially sharply.”

*** From what I hear from Persian Gulf officials, the opposite trends in crude and refined products is intentional, with an effort to prioritize the later. *** 
 
@Vortexa puts refined products exports in the first half of November at >4.5m b/d, or about 70% of pre-war level (2025 average). I hear similar numbers from trade houses and national oil companies in the region.

Put crude and refined products together, and Nov 1-15 data suggests overall oil exports are running at the same level of September, but lower than October. Sure enough, Iranian attacks against oil tankers are having an impact, but they are not deterring exporters.

US net equity inflows are up to ~3.0% of GDP, their highest on record in data going back to the 1980s.

Net equity inflows measure foreign purchases of US stocks minus US investors' purchases of foreign equities.

This figure has risen nearly +5.0 percentage points since the 2022 bear market low.

Meanwhile, net debt inflows, which measure foreign purchases of US debt securities, such as Treasuries minus US purchases of foreign debt securities, are down to ~1.8%, their lowest since 2022.

As a result, net equity inflows have surpassed net debt inflows as a % of GDP by the widest margin since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

In other words, foreign investors are increasingly directing money towards US equities rather than US bonds.

Overseas demand for US equities has never been this strong.

read this if you believe “nvidia will do just fine without jensen”

if meta no longer had zuck as ceo, they’d never risk tens of billions to build muse (fastest growing ai app in the world btw)

no ceo appointed by the board would ever have the political capital to do that

if meta was set up to get rid of zuck after, say, the cambridge analytica scandal, they’d just hire a ceo in a suit to talk about instagram ad growth quarter over quarter (note that zuck doesn’t even mention this stuff ever) and swiftly turn meta into an irrelevant dinosaur

if amazon wasn’t led by jeff bezos at the time, we’d never have AWS. amazon would still be an online book store (but the biggest one!). no board-appointed ceo could ever take that risk (shareholders hated it at the time)

tim cook may have grown apple to be the largest company in the world, but there isn’t a single soul on the planet who doesn’t wonder “what if” jobs was still alive. he was obsessed with siri, would he have led the first AI breakthrough? would he have beaten elon to self driving cars? we’ll never know. but hey, we got macbooks with a touch screen!

if walt disney was replaced early on do you really think the board would have approved disneyland?!

for its first 10 years, netflix was a physical dvd rental service. you think if they weren’t founder-led they’d make the risky switch to streaming?

nvidia was only able to take the insane risks that it did over the years thanks to jensen. replacing him means settling with the way things are today. if you think the world will no longer change from here on out then that’s fine!

tweets.text: Common sense says that you shouldn’t buy any drug that isn’t alcohol/tobacco from a gas station
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
This is wild...

Big stories in NYT today, where reporters went to an Atlanta gas station convenience store to test cannabinoids and other newfangled, candy-colored drugs. 

They bought a THC joint sold by a company called FVKD Exotics. The packaging lists THC-P and CBG as main ingredients. Testing found neither chemical in the product—but NYT did find an illegally unlisted intoxicant. 

Seeking further information, they contacted the company directly and found the address provided was ... uh, actually a UPS store that had no knowledge of the company.

I don't think you have to be a prude to think that the current state of widespread hallucinogens/cannabis/Kratom productization could possibly use a little more care and oversight. It would nice if the Trump administration were 1/100th as interested in regulating this stuff as they are at outlawing mRNA vaccines.

#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Myriad Uranium. Please do your own research.

#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Myriad Uranium. Please do your own research.

the greatest buying opportunities always show up when they seem least obvious.

Collector Crypt's gacha volumes have dropped significantly. so did the solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp price.

I think a few things clearly aren't priced in, which is why I believe this is one of the most undervalued onchain businesses in the industry right now:

- these charts only show onchain revenue. as the partner network building on their API grows and they verticalize the whole stack, a growing share of the business happens offchain. that's hard to verify from the outside, but in my view the business is doing better than these charts suggest.

- you think Ripmart is priced in. it isn't. people understand the value proposition, but hardly anyone grasps the scale of what's being built. I expect it to onboard a huge number of users within the first few weeks, most of them without even realizing they're onchain. probably the single most important thing for the business and its marketplace, and the market gives it zero credit.

- the indices were announced in the worst possible market and sentiment, so they were mostly overlooked. I'd also argue most people don't yet understand what they'll look like and why it potentially even could grow into their most profitable offering. together with Ripmart they're a gamechanger: they broaden the product suite and make the business less dependent on gacha revenue alone, which has been the biggest question mark for more conservative investors.

to sum it up: even on these sharply lower numbers, they still generate more than $70M in annualized net revenue, with one of the most profitable, obsessed and sharp teams in the space.

on top of that, more than a third of the supply sits in the treasury, and the team has confirmed those tokens only enter circulation for something clearly accretive to the business, like strategic acquisitions.

adjust for that and the effective valuation is around $200M imo. the market is pricing in the worst case for solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp, a Pokémon bubble bursting and revenue in decline, but none of the biggest catalysts and bull cases.

the most obvious non-obvious opportunity out there imo.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | MONDAY, NOVEMBER 23
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

Saturday’s tanker attack near Hormuz put oil at the top of my screen. By 04:23 GMT, Brent was trading at $92.67, just ten cents above Friday’s close. Silver had a much bigger morning.

🥈 Spot silver jumped 4.1% to $42.86/oz and gold rebounded 2.9% to $3,635.80/oz by 07:21 GMT. Traders still priced in a quarter-point Fed hike for December, but bets on a half-point hike had faded. If the dollar and the US 10-year real yield climb in New York, can gold hold $3,600?

☢️ Uranium ended last week near US$90/lb. In Australia, Paladin’s retail share offer opened today at A$7.80. The stock rose 2.9% and still closed at A$6.02. Shareholders could buy the same shares on the ASX for 23% less than the offer price. That’s why I’d wait for the result before counting the extra A$50 million.

🔶 Yesterday I asked how long Shanghai buyers would keep paying up for copper. This morning, as imports arrived, the average premium for immediate delivery fell 42%, from 5,800 to 3,350 yuan per tonne over December futures. LME copper briefly slipped below US$12,000/t.

🌏 India’s factory PMI hit a nine-month high of 56.0. The eurozone reports at 09:00 GMT and the US at 14:45 GMT. I’ll be looking at new orders for clues to copper demand. For gold, the week’s bigger test is Wednesday’s US PCE inflation reading.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Metals Pulse.

Nogen må stoppe den absurde voksenbørnehave, som skraldeafdelingen er ved at udvikle sig til.

Husk, at der er ansat 0,5 skraldebureaukrat per skraldemand. Det er det glade vanvid.

GeneDx ( $WGS ): The bipartisan legislation mentioned in Senator Klobuchar’s post below, published Friday after market close, could be the game changer GeneDx investors have been waiting for.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. 𝗜𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗺𝗯𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

GeneDx is a leader in pediatric genomic diagnostics. The company helps diagnose rare genetic diseases in children, sometimes ending years of uncertainty for families who have been going from one hospital to another looking for answers.

𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗞𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗧 𝗔𝗡 𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘.

The demand is already there. GeneDx reported 25% year-over-year growth in exome and genome testing volumes in Q3, with full-year growth guidance of at least 28%. More doctors are ordering genomic tests, more patients are being diagnosed, and the clinical value of this technology is becoming increasingly clear.

But here is the problem.

𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Approximately 48% of its insured outpatient testing volume comes from Medicaid patients, yet whole genome sequencing is covered by Medicaid in only 25 states.

Think about this for a moment. You have a company with rapidly growing demand for its services, but the payment system has not caught up with the technology.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗦𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚.

If passed as described, it would make qualifying pediatric genomic sequencing a mandatory Medicaid benefit, allow doctors to use it as a first-tier diagnostic test, and require separate payment for hospital testing.

This is not simply about increasing the number of tests.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

Today, every additional test creates clinical value, but it does not necessarily translate into money collected.

With broader coverage and a clearer reimbursement framework, growing testing volumes could finally translate into growing cash collections.

And that is a completely different business.

Imagine a company growing testing volumes by 25% annually while struggling to get paid. Now imagine the same company with broader reimbursement, better collection rates, and a much larger addressable market.

Revenue growth could accelerate without requiring an equivalent increase in testing volume. Fixed costs could be spread across more paid tests, improving margins and potentially cash flow.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵. 𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀.

Of course, coverage does not guarantee payment. Reimbursement rates, implementation, and GeneDx’s own execution would still matter.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗔𝗗𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

This is an important step toward improving health outcomes and saving lives.

𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Approximately 48% of its insured outpatient testing volume comes from Medicaid patients, yet whole genome sequencing is covered by Medicaid in only 25 states.

Think about this for a moment. You have a company with rapidly growing demand for its services, but the payment system has not caught up with the technology.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗦𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚.

If passed as described, it would make qualifying pediatric genomic sequencing a mandatory Medicaid benefit, allow doctors to use it as a first-tier diagnostic test, and require separate payment for hospital testing.

This is not simply about increasing the number of tests.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

Today, every additional test creates clinical value, but it does not necessarily translate into money collected.

With broader coverage and a clearer reimbursement framework, growing testing volumes could finally translate into growing cash collections.

And that is a completely different business.

Imagine a company growing testing volumes by 25% annually while struggling to get paid. Now imagine the same company with broader reimbursement, better collection rates, and a much larger addressable market.

Revenue growth could accelerate without requiring an equivalent increase in testing volume. Fixed costs could be spread across more paid tests, improving margins and potentially cash flow.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵. 𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀.

Of course, coverage does not guarantee payment. Reimbursement rates, implementation, and GeneDx’s own execution would still matter.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗔𝗗𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗖𝗞.

$WGS traded near $100 just a few months ago, when investors were hoping its financial performance would improve. Today it trades around $46.

Corvex Management and Casdin Capital maintained their reported positions through Q3, even when the stock was trading near $100. Deep Track Capital, another specialist healthcare fund, recently disclosed approximately 6% ownership.

These are investors with considerable experience in the industry.

My thesis is that the market has been valuing GeneDx as a company with strong clinical demand but serious problems turning that demand into cash.

𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.

One with rapidly growing testing volumes, a difficult-to-replicate database, broader insurance coverage, improving collections, and potentially much better operating leverage.

That combination could justify a significant re-rating.

The bill is not guaranteed to pass, and GeneDx still has serious operational problems to solve. But the potential change in its economics is enormous.

I cannot imagine that 10 years from now, parents will still spend years going from hospital to hospital trying to understand what is wrong with their children when the technology already exists to provide answers much earlier.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

Full disclaimer: This will be my last post about $WGS until the next earnings report. Unfortunately, I started buying at much higher prices, and I doubled my position today.

I don’t think there’s any rush to buy. Take your time, do your own research, and see if it makes sense to you. In fact, I would recommend not rushing into anything I write about. There’s never a reason to rush and buy a stock just because I mention it.

But I do think this news could be a game changer for the company. Hopefully, we get to see round two.

Thank you to everyone who joined us in Miami for our inaugural Investing Through the Cycles (ITC) conference.

To the attendees who traveled from all around the world, it meant a lot to me that you made the trip. Some of my favorite moments were between sessions, when I finally got to meet people in person who have been part of the ITC community for years.

To our speakers, thank you for making the time to join us and for sharing how you think about markets. One of the reasons I wanted to put this conference together was to hear from people who can look at the same market and come to very different conclusions. I appreciated how willing you were to explain your thinking and challenge one another’s views.

A special thank you to Dana Howell @thedanahowell  for organizing the conference. Dana thought through so many of the little details that made people feel welcome. I saw how much care went into bringing the weekend together, and I’m grateful for all of it.

I’m glad we got to spend the weekend together, and I hope to see you again next year.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
$hype is cheap again.

the price fell 36% since september. $98 → $62.5. but the revenue didn't.

hyperliquid revenue:

> 90 days before the top: $164M
> last 90 days: $221M (+35%)
> november: $2.6M a day, the highest of 2026

all of it is used to buy back hype. and a lower price means each dollar buys more tokens.

hype bought back:

> 90 days before the top: 2.31M
> last 90 days: 2.73M (+18%)
> november: ~36K a day, the most since march

so for $1 of yearly revenue you now pay:

> hype at the top: $33
> hype today: $17
> cme: $25
> nasdaq: $28
> robinhood: $29

another way to see it: at this pace, buybacks equal 6% of hype's market cap a year. at the top it was 3%. cme gives back ~3.5% to its shareholders.

more revenue, more buybacks, lower price.

on these numbers, hype is undervalued.

I don't like how bullish the bulls are becoming

I also don't like how this bounce looks

I also don't like how everyone is bringing out the "this is the most extreme selling in years!" and "10-sigma event" to justify buying the dip

Generally, I think that you a strong BTFD scenario is made when stocks correct sharply in an irrational scenario and can be argued to be broadly undervalued when you're in an environment that is rather accomodative to stocks - for example, the Iran War, or Liberation Day, both of which were one-off macro events that spooked the market in an otherwise ok-environment at the beginning of the bull run

However, at these levels, if you ask me there is no irrational selling going on here. What is irrational about selling after every stock has done multiples from the bottom? 

My intuition is telling me that it's ok to DCA here for long term positions, and ok to play the bounce, but it is not ok to bet the farm on some sort of V-reversal here - UNLESS we get a major catalyst to justify that ; then yes, I will agree it's extremely +EV to do so

But if nothing changes, and we keep getting the same shit, then it seems pretty meh.

The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world. 

The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%. 

Tell me why I am wrong.

That isn't what End to End encryption means. 

It just means the payload is encrypted on the user's machine, it can travel across several intermediaries until it reaches the endpoint (i.e., privy's servers). 

It is then decrypted by the recipient. 

Importantly, it should _also_ be authenticated, so when the user encrypts the message they know the public key indeed belongs to the recipient (i.e., privy) and not anyone else.
